name: Moyamoya disease
aliases: spontaneous occlusion of the circle of Willis

reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / cerebrovascular surgery literature
clinicalPearls: Progressive stenosis and occlusion of the terminal internal carotid arteries and proximal circle of Willis
A fragile network of dilated basal collateral vessels produces the characteristic angiographic puff of smoke appearance
Bimodal presentation: children typically present with ischaemia and adults may present with intracranial haemorrhage from fragile collaterals
Hyperventilation, as with crying in children, can precipitate transient ischaemic symptoms by lowering carbon dioxide
The RNF213 susceptibility variant is strongly associated, particularly in East Asian populations
Moyamoya syndrome describes the same angiographic pattern secondary to conditions such as sickle cell disease, neurofibromatosis, or prior radiation
Surgical revascularisation to augment collateral flow is the mainstay of definitive treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Moyamoya disease is a chronic, progressive, non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory steno-occlusive arteriopathy of the distal internal carotid arteries and their proximal branches. Intimal thickening from smooth muscle cell proliferation and luminal narrowing reduce anterior circulation flow, prompting the growth of fragile lenticulostriate and leptomeningeal collateral networks that give the smoky angiographic appearance. These collaterals are prone to ischaemic failure and, being thin-walled and under haemodynamic stress, to rupture and haemorrhage. Genetic susceptibility, notably RNF213 variants, underlies many idiopathic cases.
additionalDifferentials: Intracranial vasculitis or primary angiitis of the CNS
additionalInvestigations: Digital subtraction angiography as the gold standard to demonstrate steno-occlusion and collateral networks
MRI and MR angiography showing basal collaterals and ischaemic or haemorrhagic lesions
Cerebral perfusion and vascular reserve studies to guide revascularisation
Testing for secondary causes such as sickle cell disease and RNF213 genotyping where appropriate
Assessment for associated conditions like neurofibromatosis or prior cranial irradiation
redFlags: Intracranial haemorrhage from rupture of fragile collateral vessels
Recurrent transient ischaemic attacks or completed strokes
Ischaemic symptoms provoked by hyperventilation, especially in children
reference.prognosis: Untreated moyamoya tends to progress with recurrent ischaemic or haemorrhagic events and cumulative neurological deficit; surgical revascularisation can reduce stroke risk and stabilise the disease, though outcome depends on the stage at diagnosis.
pitfalls: Mistaking the arteriopathy for atherosclerosis and withholding revascularisation assessment
Aggressive blood pressure lowering that compromises collateral-dependent perfusion
Overlooking secondary causes when labelling the pattern as idiopathic disease
Failing to protect against hypocapnia during anaesthesia, which can precipitate ischaemia
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Surgical revascularisation, by direct superficial-temporal-to-middle-cerebral-artery bypass or indirect procedures such as encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis, is the definitive treatment to restore perfusion and reduce stroke risk
Give antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin to reduce ischaemic events in the ischaemic-predominant form
Avoid precipitants of ischaemia including hyperventilation, hypotension, hypocapnia and dehydration, and maintain euvolaemia and normocapnia in the perioperative period
Identify and treat secondary (moyamoya syndrome) causes, for example transfusion for sickle cell disease
Provide stroke rehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy after ischaemic or haemorrhagic events
Monitor with serial angiographic and cerebral perfusion imaging for disease progression
Consider RNF213 genotyping and counselling, particularly in East Asian patients, and assess relatives
Escalate urgently for new transient ischaemic attacks, stroke or intracranial haemorrhage
